text: Meridian Polymers supplied cosmetic resins to regional brands. The disputed material was a compilation of the customers who buy each product line. Veyron Beauty later entered the same market. The record describes the compilation as listing account names and volumes without reference to any technical process.

Plaintiff Meridian Polymers maintained records identifying its specialty suppliers by region for sourcing polymer feedstock. Defendant Veyron Beauty obtained a comparable set of supplier names through ordinary commercial contact. The materials at issue contained no formulas or engineering data, only the identities and locations of third-party vendors.

Veyron Beauty commenced a beauty-packaging line in 2019. Meridian Polymers had previously kept the roster of distributor accounts and contact persons used for its resin sales. The roster named handling agents and their phone numbers. No manufacturing specification appeared in the documents reviewed by the court.

In the early 2000s Meridian Polymers generated spreadsheets of buyer identities and order histories across its polymer divisions. Veyron Beauty thereafter compiled a similar buyer list. The spreadsheets recorded client names and purchase dates. The information did not describe any internal production method or proprietary design.

Defendant Veyron Beauty received from a former associate the list of vendors it sources components from, as used by Meridian Polymers in its compound operations. The list set out company names and addresses. It reflected procurement relationships rather than a protected technical process.

Meridian Polymers, a resin producer, held account records naming its wholesale purchasers for the year 2015. Veyron Beauty later marketed to those same accounts. The records consisted of purchaser names and shipment totals. The dispute centered on whether such business relationships qualified as protectable subject matter.

Veyron Beauty reviewed a directory of its supplier relationships and terms that Meridian Polymers had assembled for polymer sourcing. The document identified counterparties and agreed delivery conditions. It contained no laboratory results. The parties described the entries as standard commercial contacts.

Plaintiff Meridian Polymers created files identifying which retailers carry the line of its consumer resin products. Defendant Veyron Beauty obtained an equivalent retailer index. The files stated store names and regional placement. There was no inclusion of chemical formulations or apparatus drawings in the files.

In the early 2010s, Vantor Gaming acquired documents from BlueFern Genetics that contained the list of vendors it sources components from within the cosmetics sector. The pages identified each supplier and the types of ingredients procured. No technical specifications or manufacturing steps appeared in the files.

Plaintiff BlueFern Genetics had compiled records identifying its specialty suppliers by region for oil & gas drilling-fluid additives. Defendant Vantor Gaming came into possession of the spreadsheets listing those firms. The entries showed only names, locations, and supply categories, not any engineering data.

During 2008, BlueFern Genetics prepared a roster of distributor accounts and contact persons for its gaming-related testing kits. Vantor Gaming received the roster after a corporate split. The document set out account names and phone numbers of the distributors, with no product designs included.

Vantor Gaming reviewed files from BlueFern Genetics that were account records naming its wholesale purchasers in the biotech market. The records stated which hospitals bought reagents and their volume tiers. The information was limited to buyer identities and did not reveal any proprietary compound.

BlueFern Genetics formerly kept spreadsheets of buyer identities and order histories for cosmetic raw-material supply. Defendant Vantor Gaming held these sheets following an asset purchase. They recorded client names and past purchase dates, presenting commercial relationships rather than a technical process.

A 1999 internal workbook of BlueFern Genetics described a compilation of the customers who buy each product line in oil & gas services. Vantor Gaming inherited the workbook through a merger. The tables matched product codes to client firms and omitted any operational know-how.

BlueFern Genetics generated files identifying which retailers carry the line of biotech sampling tools. Vantor Gaming accessed those files in 2015 as part of a transition. The files mapped store names to territories and contained no research protocols or chemical methods.

Vantor Gaming came upon a directory of its supplier relationships and terms that BlueFern Genetics had used in cosmetics packaging. The booklet named fragrance suppliers and payment windows. It was a plain record of who supplied what, not a recipe or confined manufacturing technique.

During 2018, Redgate Software came across files identifying which retailers carry the line of Cascade Biotech in the medical devices sector. The contents stated store names and territory assignments. The disclosed material concerned placement with buyers and not the concealed steps of production.

Records identifying its specialty suppliers by region were held by Cascade Biotech before Redgate Software obtained them in a 2015 transaction. The sheets paired geographic zones with vendor names. They outlined procurement channels and remained silent on the techniques applied inside the plaintiff's factories.

The roster of distributor accounts and contact persons at Cascade Biotech passed to Redgate Software through a broker. Listed were regional handlers and their representatives in the logistics field. Such a business directory illustrated who moved the goods, not how the items were fabricated.

Redgate Software in 2012 received spreadsheets of buyer identities and order histories from Cascade Biotech's legacy system. Cascade Biotech's list of vendors it sources components from was shared with Redgate Software by a third party in the robotics supply chain. The schedule named outside workshops and part numbers. It revealed sourcing structure and contained no description of the plaintiff's build routines.
